title: Bigger Kitchen, More Brunch: Wild Poppy Cafe Expands at The Barlow in Sebastopol
summary:
After building a following at their cozy west Sebastopol cafe, Martin and Danielle Maigaard have opened a larger restaurant and marketplace with sunny patio dining, brunch favorites and room to bake.

The post Bigger Kitchen, More Brunch: Wild Poppy Cafe Expands at The Barlow in Sebastopol appeared first on Sonoma Magazine.
content:
For 22 years, Martin and Danielle Maigaard dreamed of opening a restaurant with a spacious kitchen, room to bake, ample parking and an artisan marketplace bigger than a closet.

Instead, in 2024, they fell for a quirky-cool roadhouse in west Sebastopol that had none of those things. Wild Poppy Cafe, at 9890 Bodega Highway, was small, a little out of the way and simply too charming to resist.

“We wanted to start small and make sure it was received well,” Martin said.

It was. The cafe became a rarity in the restaurant business: a runaway success. Perhaps it was the quiet creekside patio, the fresh pastries or the beans and greens that became a signature dish. (This is west county, after all.)

Still, the couple dreamed of a little more space — especially in the kitchen and the parking lot.

Their new Wild Poppy Cafe and Marketplace at The Barlow delivers on both counts. Open for just a few weeks, the 3,500-square-foot former brewery has been drawing crowds for brunch and lunch, with diners settling onto the sunny patio over Korean chicken rice bowls, tacos and French toast topped with apple compote.

The Barlow is hardly short on good food and drink. Sarmentine turns out pastries, Taylor Lane serves coffee, and Acre Pizza, Sushi Kosho and Genero’s offer plenty of dining options. But Wild Poppy fills a different niche: a relaxed, brunch-friendly gathering place for Wednesday morning meetups, work-from-home days when you don’t actually want to work from home, and leisurely weekend meals.

“You walk in and it feels like home,” Martin said. “We wanted it to feel like we were hosting, like a backyard gathering or a dinner party.”

Danielle was quick to add another ingredient to the formula.

“And everyone we hire has to be nice. Customers see that, and I think that’s really helped us along.”

A new location, a familiar menu

Opening a second restaurant was no walk in the park. It was more like six months of welding torches and saws.

Martin, who has spent years renovating homes, handled much of the construction himself at the original cafe on Bodega Highway. At The Barlow, he took the same do-it-yourself approach, working without a contractor. The project took longer than expected, but the savings made the extra effort worthwhile.

The new cafe retains customer favorites, including Baja fish tacos and Cosmic Queso nachos, while adding a handful of dishes: fancy toast, salads, a salmon burger and rice bowls.

The marketplace brings together local products and fair-trade goods, including pottery, spices, blankets, napkins, towels and Wild Poppy merchandise. A deli case is being stocked with grab-and-go soups, dips and salads.

Coffee and espresso drinks share the menu with beer, wine and a sunny turmeric lemonade made in-house. Save room for the housemade gluten-free peanut butter chocolate chip cookies.

Restaurant success stories have become harder to come by. But the Maigaards appear to have found a formula that works in west Sonoma County.

That’s something worth raising a mimosa to.

Details: Wild Poppy Cafe & Market is at 6780 McKinley St., Suite 160, Sebastopol. Open 10 a.m. to 3 p.m. Wednesday through Monday and closed Tuesday.

Wild Poppy Creekside is at 9890 Bodega Highway, Sebastopol. Open 10 a.m. to 3 p.m. Thursday through Sunday. thewildpoppycafe.com

title: We Had Breakfast With Sonoma County’s Smashburger King
summary:
Smashburger maestro Justin Haley and dining editor Heather Irwin meet for breakfast, talking about food, life, love and favorite restaurants.

The post We Had Breakfast With Sonoma County’s Smashburger King appeared first on Sonoma Magazine.
content:
Justin Haley is Sonoma County’s king of smashburgers. Not all kings wear crowns. Some wear T-shirts and chef’s pants.

You’ll usually find Haley, a gentle giant, working the flattop beneath a black pop-up tent at breweries, farmers markets and local events, turning out the thin burgers he’s perfected over the years, with crunchy cheese and char around the edges. But the real draw is the neon-orange sauce that squeezes out from every crevice.

It’s not quite Thousand Island dressing, and it’s not quite barbecue sauce. Rich with spices and a hint of smoke, it’s something entirely its own. Haley won’t tell you the recipe, but he will tell you the inspiration.

“I wanted something alarmingly orange colored,” he said. “My goal was the Nickelodeon orange. But with no dyes. I wanted that nostalgic color. And it needed to pair well with wine and beer — we’re in Sonoma County after all.”

Haley also loves working the register and holding court with customers. Children are particularly fascinated by the sauce’s improbable hue, and he often goes home with their drawings.

He’s equally generous with his fellow food vendors, sharing spare napkins, giving away burgers and lending an extra set of hands when someone is in the weeds, even during a heated food competition. He usually wins anyway. That’s just the kind of guy Haley is.

After a busy weekend of events and another People’s Choice Award, this time at the Smash Bash smashburger showdown at Shady Oak Barrel House, we met for breakfast at one of his favorite spots, Marvin’s of Cotati, to talk burgers, breakfast and the pleasures of cooking in Sonoma County.

Let’s meet for breakfast

Even on a Tuesday morning, Marvin’s is packed. Tucked into a quiet strip mall, it’s the kind of place you might drive past without a second thought. Locals know better.

The restaurant is a destination for hearty steak and eggs, pancakes and its specialty, chilaquiles: crisp tortilla chips piled with eggs, chorizo and a deep-brown mole, a smoky, slightly sweet chile sauce made in-house.

Over two generous plates of chilaquiles that threaten to overpower both our appetite and our resolve, Haley and I dig in.

First off, where did the name Thanks for the Invite come from?

My wife, Paige, and I spent months traveling across California looking for the perfect burger. We tried everything. Big cities, small towns, roadside stops. We paid attention and started to notice what made certain burgers stand out and why others were easy to forget. It was not about doing the most. It was about doing it right.

We practiced a lot back home, trying to get our own burger just right, and then invited friends over to try them. Everyone loved them and ended up saying, “Thanks for the invite!”

Why did you pick Marvin’s for our breakfast?

It’s a classic breakfast staple. They aren’t trying to do anything crazy. From the jams and jellies to salsa and mole, everything is made in-house by the family, something you don’t see much anymore.

What does breakfast look like for you on a normal day?

I don’t eat breakfast. It’s rare, but when I do, I like to kinda go all out and order pancakes to share for the table. Every time.

What’s better: Tacos or burritos?

I love them both, but I’m a nacho guy at heart. When I was 11 years old, I used to write nacho reviews. The old Rafa’s in Cotati used to bake enchilada sauce into their chips and cheese, and I think about that pretty often.

What’s something you love about cooking in Sonoma County?

The people! I feel like Sonoma County’s food community is actually massive. Whenever I have a weird idea, I know there’s always somebody nearby who’s going to try it. I feel like the community supports locals so much, something you can’t really find in a big city.

What are you obsessed with right now, food or otherwise?

Salads. I don’t look like it, but I’m a sucker for a salad. Also, my wife, Paige.

What’s your favorite restaurant or chef in Sonoma County?

Diavola. They just do everything so absolutely right, and at a price point you can’t beat. I’m a huge fan of sharing plates, and I think that’s just a perfect spot to do it. Also, the Gun Club (same owners) has our favorite smashburger (besides our own).

What would you eat for your last meal? Because I think this Mexican hot chocolate from Marvin’s is on my list.

I’d love some toasted sourdough bread, butter with a little extra salt, a little local honey, and some ripe peaches and pluots under a tree in a field in Sonoma County with the love of my life.

What food trends do you hate?

Height on food. Like, I don’t want a tall sandwich or tall burger. Flatten that thing out and make it wider. My mouth can’t open that much!

Who should I interview next?

Beryl Adler of Acorn Cafe in Healdsburg. That guy is magic, and he’s a massive inspiration.

Details about where to find Justin and Thanks for the Invite can be found at instagram.com/thanksfortheinvite.ca.

title: From Fries to Fine Dining: The Greek at Appellation Healdsburg
summary:
Food truck chef Dino Moniodis trades gyros and fries for five-course Greek dinners at Folia in Healdsburg, showing off his fine-dining chops.

The post From Fries to Fine Dining: The Greek at Appellation Healdsburg appeared first on Sonoma Magazine.
content:
Dino Moniodis can turn out a mean lamb gyro, falafel plate and seasoned fries from the tiny kitchen of his Greek food truck. Give him a state-of-the-art kitchen, a live-fire grill and room to experiment, though, and the 34-year-old chef is in his element.

After years of cooking Greek street food, Moniodis is getting a chance to showcase his fine-dining skills at Folia Bar + Kitchen in Healdsburg, trading takeout containers for five-course dinners.

“It’s pretty amazing,” he said as he prepared for his Monday night dinner series, The Greek at Appellation Healdsburg.

The pop-up series began in late September and has sold out every week, Moniodis said. The $85 dinner begins with family-style mezze, including phyllo-wrapped feta drizzled with honey, roasted tomatoes, kataifi-wrapped prawns and tender octopus.

“It’s the way a Greek table actually works,” he said.

A family tradition of cooking

Moniodis spent much of his childhood summers on the Greek island of Chios, working at his family’s taverna. Sharing food around the table was tradition, and it remains central to how he wants guests to experience his cooking.

The main course might be a wood-fired pork or lamb chop, depending on the week, accompanied by roasted eggplant, lentils and a charred apple-and-lemon beurre blanc. It’s good enough to make sharing feel like an unreasonable demand — I guarded my plate from wandering forks and used a piece of leftover pita to mop up the last of the sauce.

It’s the kind of cooking Moniodis rarely gets to do in his 10-by-10-foot food truck kitchen, where elaborate plating and more ambitious techniques are hard to pull off. Trained in kitchens across Sonoma County, including several years at Willi’s Wine Bar, he’s got the chops, classic sauces and knife skills down. What he has lacked is the space and opportunity to spread his wings.

“I’ve had the training, but not the platform,” he said.

Greek food is personal

Moniodis’ summers in Greece remain a touchstone, a mix of playing on the beach with cousins and learning to cook at the taverna. Later, while caring for his father during a serious illness, the two discussed opening a Greek restaurant.

After his father’s death in 2018, Moniodis decided to pursue that dream. He launched Dino’s Greek Food in 2019.

The business led to other ventures, including Zimi on Mission in Santa Rosa, where he paired Greek staples like spanakopita, dolmas and pastitsio with wood-fired pizzas. The restaurant closed after 18 months, but Moniodis was not ready to abandon the restaurant he and his father had envisioned.

An opportunity to move closer to that goal came in April, when Moniodis was named one of the North Bay Business Journal’s 40 Under 40. At the awards event, he met chef Charlie Palmer and his sons, Reed and Courtland, who are involved with Appellation Healdsburg, a culinary-focused resort that opened in September 2025. Reed leads the kitchen at Folia Bar + Kitchen, while Courtland is president of Appellation. The resort is also home to Andys Beeline Rooftop Bar.

Moniodis introduced himself and pitched an idea: a Monday night series devoted to Greek cooking at Folia. The Palmers agreed, and The Greek debuted in September. Charlie Palmer has confirmed that the series will continue into the fall.

“He’s been very lenient, just letting me do whatever I want to do,” Moniodis said.

The arrangement has offered more than a chance to cook. Moniodis has also gained a closer look at the business of fine dining, from menu development and staffing to marketing and reservations. Unlike running his own kitchens, he now has an established team to rely on.

“It feels like I’m running a small restaurant,” he said. “It’s nice to be part of a team and lean on people and get back into the kitchen.”

For now, Moniodis is cooking the food he loves in the setting he has long wanted. Each Monday brings him a little closer to the Greek restaurant he and his father dreamed of opening. One dinner at a time.

Details: The Greek at Appellation offers five-course dinners for $85 per person, with Greek wines available separately. Reservations are available through OpenTable. 101 Dovetail Lane, Healdsburg, 707-723-2130, foliabarandkitchen.com

title: Inside J&M’s Midtown Cafe, a Santa Rosa Breakfast Favorite
summary:
At J&M’s Midtown Cafe, longtime chef Joel Shaw puts his own spin on a beloved Santa Rosa breakfast spot without messing with the dishes regulars love.

The post Inside J&M’s Midtown Cafe, a Santa Rosa Breakfast Favorite appeared first on Sonoma Magazine.
content:
When Joel and Marla Shaw bought Dierk’s Midtown Cafe in 2023, they knew better than to tamper with crowd favorites like smoked salmon hash, Gompa’s pancake breakfast and the beloved Country Benedict.

Joel Shaw had been one of those regulars before he became the owner. A longtime chef and devoted breakfast fan, he and Marla understood how much the neighborhood loved the restaurant, founded by chef Mark Dierkhising, who also opened Dierk’s Parkside Cafe.

Still, even a classic can stand a little reinvention.

Keeping the best of the past with an eye toward the future, the couple created J&M’s Midtown Cafe. For Joel, a former cook at Ramen Gaijin in Sebastopol, the kitchen became a kind of laboratory, a place to experiment with ingredients and techniques without losing sight of what brought customers through the door.

He raised the bar on the New York-style pastrami sandwich by brining the meat in-house and added one of his own diner favorites, chicken-fried steak. Seasonal hashes offer another outlet for his creativity. Recently, he worked pickled grapes into a hash, using fruit from the restaurant’s back porch. Inspired by Persian cuisine, he has his eye on pomegranates, which he’s considering adding to a duck confit.

But there’s a limit to how much he wants to change — he knows when to let a good thing be.

The cafe has been a dream come true for Joel, which made the illness that sidelined him a year ago all the more difficult. He could not lift a saucepan, let alone wash dishes or bus tables, and faced a long recovery.

The staff kept the restaurant going. Bussers picked up shifts, kitchen workers came in on their days off, and Marla and the couple’s son filled in wherever they were needed. Their efforts carried the cafe through until Joel could return to work.

Now he’s back to doing a little of everything: cooking, taking orders, clearing tables and washing dishes when the cafe gets busy, which happens often enough because regulars keep arriving for their pancake breakfasts and Benedicts.

The details

How long in business: The location has been a breakfast and brunch destination for more than a decade. The Shaws reopened it as J&M’s Midtown Cafe in 2023.

Most popular dish: The simplest dish has the biggest fan base: Two Eggs – And You’re Outta Here! comes with two eggs cooked any style, hash browns and toast.

What they can never take off the menu: The Country Benedict, a warm baguette topped with two eggs, bacon, mushrooms, spinach, oven-dried tomatoes and housemade hollandaise. A staple on the Dierk’s menu, it remains a favorite among regulars.

Fun fact: The kitchen goes through about 1,500 eggs per week, or 125 dozen.

The vibe: A relaxed neighborhood diner, with a small wraparound counter for those looking for a quick meal. Inside, there’s a steady clink of forks, friendly chatter and steaming cups of Bella Rosa coffee at nearly every table. Service is casual but attentive. Joel might be cooking, taking an order or clearing tables, depending on what the moment requires.

The chef’s favorite: Chicken-fried steak. Joel judges every diner he visits by the dish. “If it’s not good, I don’t need to go back there,” he said. His version features a crisp crust over beefsteak, finished with white country sausage gravy made with turkey broth.

The deals: Bottomless mimosas on Saturdays and Sundays. All-day happy hour Mondays and Tuesdays, with $3 off alcoholic drinks.

The price: Most dishes range from $14 to $20.

The nights: On Friday evenings, Twilight Magic, a takeout-only pop-up, takes over the cafe with crispy chicken tenders, biscuits, cute-as-a-button cakelets and super-craveable Thai tea rice pudding. Emilio Saldaña makes the oversize tenders, coating them in a secret blend of herbs and spices that would make the Colonel envious, while Dia Gutierrez handles the baking. Find more details at twilight-magic-cafe.com.

Best bets

Country Benedict ($16): The benchmark against which I measure other Benedicts. Poached eggs spill their yolks over bacon, mushrooms and spinach on a split baguette, with well-balanced hollandaise and an oven-roasted tomato adding a note of acidity.

Chicken-fried steak ($19): A diner worth its salt knows how to handle this old-school favorite, a crisp, fried steak under a blanket of sausage gravy. Plenty of places serve it, but few make everything from scratch. At J&M’s, that’s more than a point of pride. It is the point.

Smoked salmon latkes Benedict ($18): Crisp on the outside and soft on the inside, the latkes are topped with house-smoked salmon rather than lox.

French toast ($12.65): Ciabatta soaked in cinnamon custard, soft in the middle and crisp around the edges.

New York-style pastrami sandwich ($16): Not quite a Reuben, but close enough. Buttery, toasted whole-grain bread holds thinly sliced pastrami, lightly pickled red cabbage and Thousand Island-style dressing. A layer of melted Jack cheese finishes the sandwich, with just enough heat to curl the pastrami’s edges. Perfection.

J&M’s Midtown Cafe is open 7 a.m. to 1:30 p.m. Thursday through Tuesday (closed Wednesday). 1422 Fourth St., Santa Rosa. 707-545-2233, jm-midtowncafe.com

title: Where To Celebrate Halloween in Sonoma County
summary:
Halloween happenings abound this year in Sonoma County, from carnivals and costume contests to film screenings and haunted tours.

The post Where To Celebrate Halloween in Sonoma County appeared first on Sonoma Magazine.
content:
October is a time for frights and delights, when skeletons adorn front porches and jumpscares lurk around every corner. In Sonoma County, Halloween festivities span the month, with themed dinners, masquerades, costume contests and horror film festivals.

Here’s where to celebrate Halloween in Sonoma County.

Santa Rosa

Pumpkins in the Parks: A Santa Rosa Scavenger Hunt, Oct. 1-30

Throughout October, locals are invited to visit any Santa Rosa park to hunt for laminated pumpkin cutouts, which include directions on how and where to collect prizes. Prizes include a variety of treats and specials from Santa Rosa Recreation & Parks, Charles M. Schulz Museum and Snoopy’s Home Ice. An adult must be present to claim the prize. City staff will re-hide the pumpkin cutouts for others to find. The last day to collect a prize is Oct. 30. Santa Rosa parks, 707-543-3737, srcity.org

Blind Scream Haunted House, select dates from Oct. 9-31

Blind Scream, one of Sonoma County’s most thrillingly scary haunted houses, will run from 7-11 p.m. on Oct. 9, 10, 16, 17, 23, 24, 29, 30 and 31; and from 7-10 p.m. on Oct. 11, 18, 22 and 25. The theme of this year’s haunted house is “Caverns of Carnage,” which transports guests beneath a graveyard into skeleton-infested caverns where horrifying creatures and demons await. The Blackout Haunted House is back again this year, daring brave guests to navigate a creepy maze in total darkness. General admission to the haunted house is $30, admission for the blackout experience is $25, and admission to both is $40. Fast passes are available. Purchase tickets online. 98 Santa Rosa Plaza, Santa Rosa, 707-953-3909, blindscream.com

Santa Rosa Zombie Crawl, Oct. 10

Blind Scream will host the city’s Zombie Crawl, a spooky bar crawl featuring Halloween-themed cocktails and specials, starting at 5:30 p.m. Oct. 10. Check in at the Blind Scream Haunted House between 5-5:30 p.m. to collect a wristband and crawl map. The recommended route starts at Shady Oak Brewing Company and traverses through downtown Santa Rosa. Other participating businesses include Ausiello’s, Belly Left Coast, J & A Lounge and La Rosa Tequileria. Tickets are $40; purchase tickets online. Hosted by Blind Scream, 98 Santa Rosa Plaza, Santa Rosa, 707-953-3909, blindscream.com

Halloween at the Flamingo, Oct. 10, 18, 30, 31

The Vintage Space music and events lounge at Santa Rosa’s Flamingo Resort & Spa will host a number of 21-and-over Halloween events throughout the month. 2777 Fourth St., Santa Rosa, vintagespacesr.com

A Halloween dance party and costume contest will be held from 10 p.m. to 3 a.m. Oct. 10. Local singer-songwriter Erica Ambrin will host the party, which will include music by DJ Lady Char and DJ Dyops, burlesque by Joey Vayda, local vendors, a photo booth and more. There will also be a costume contest with first place awarded a one-night stay at The Flamingo. The event is the official Petaluma Pride after-party and is an inclusive space for all. Tickets are $20, plus fees. Purchase tickets on Eventbrite.

Ritmo y Pasión Dance will host a Halloween Bachata Party from 7:30 p.m. to 1 a.m. on Oct. 18. The party will include a dance class starting at 8 p.m. with instructor Isa; DJ Edge spinning bachata, salsa, and cumbia; and a costume contest with prizes for the best looks. There will be a full bar and drink specials available. Pre-sale tickets are $15 and tickets at the door are $20. Purchase tickets online.

A Flamingo Fright Night costume party will be held from 8 p.m. to 1:30 a.m. on Oct. 30. Starting at 9 p.m., Northern California party band Pop Fiction will play dance hits from the 1970s through the 2000s. Costumes are highly encouraged. Tickets are $20 in advance and $25 on the day of the show, plus fees. Purchase tickets on Eventbrite.

A Halloween Rave will be held from 9 p.m. to 2 a.m. Oct. 31. The party will include house music by guest DJs played all night, local vendors, games, a full bar, lasers and an immersive sound system. Advance tickets are $20 and tickets at the door are $25, plus fees. Purchase tickets on Eventbrite.

Midnight at the Masquerade, Oct. 16

Vinarosa Resort & Spa will host Midnight at the Masquerade, a murder mystery dinner party, from 6-9 p.m. Oct. 16 at its John Ash restaurant. The evening will feature a four-course dinner paired with wines from Mercury Wine alongside a murder mystery for guests to solve. The menu includes roasted beet salad, kanpachi crudo, fried quail and chocolate cremeux. Masquerade-inspired attire is encouraged. Tickets are $200 per person, plus fees and gratuity. Purchase tickets and reserve a spot on OpenTable. 4330 Barnes Road, Santa Rosa, 707-527-7687, vinarosaresort.com/dining/john-ash

Halloween at Coddingtown, Oct. 17, 29

In addition to fun Halloween displays set up at Coddingtown all month long, the mall will host a Card Show Halloween Special from 10 a.m. to 6 p.m. Oct. 17, and a Halloween Spooktacular from 5-7 p.m. Oct. 29.

The card show will include trading cards of various sorts, from “Pokémon” and “Magic: The Gathering” to “Riftbound” and sports cards. There will be Halloween activities, giveaways and memorabilia on display. Entry is free and guests are encouraged to bring their collections and dress up. Reserve a spot on Eventbrite.

The Halloween Spooktacular will include trick-or-treating, a haunted house, face painting, costume contests, games and activities, and arts and crafts with the Sonoma County Library. Entry is free and costumes are encouraged. Coddingtown Shopping Center, 1300 Coddingtown Center, Santa Rosa, 707-978-5800, codding.com

Family FUNtaz Night at Children’s Museum, Oct. 22-23

As the Children’s Museum of Sonoma County undergoes an expansion project, it will invite families for a Family FUNtaz Night, Oct. 22, in lieu of its annual kid-friendly Halloween event, FUNtazmagoria. The event will take place from 4:30-8 p.m. Oct. 22 and from 3-8 p.m. Oct. 23 at the museum. It will include spooky crafts, creepy science experiments, food for purchase from local food trucks and wine and beer for purchase for adults. Costumes are encouraged. General admission is $22, member tickets are $11 and entry is free for infants 11 months and younger. Purchase tickets online. 1835 W. Steele Lane, Santa Rosa, 707-546-4069, cmosc.org

The Rocky Horror Show at California Theatre, Oct. 22, 23, 24

Santa Rosa’s California Theatre is doing the time warp again with three productions of Richard O’Brien’s 1973 musical The Rocky Horror Show, presented by THTR Productions, on Oct. 22, 23 and 24. Doors and bar open at 7 p.m. and showtime runs from 8-10 p.m. Costumes are highly encouraged. General admission is $60. Learn more and purchase tickets online. 528 Seventh St., Santa Rosa, 707-664-7529, caltheatre.com

Halloween at Howarth, Oct. 24

Santa Rosa’s 20th annual Halloween at Howarth will take place from 11:30 a.m. to 2:30 p.m., Oct. 24, at Howarth Park. Children ages 12 and under are welcome to trick-or-treat through the park at treat stations hosted by local businesses. The event will also include a fun zone with face painting, a photo booth, train and pony rides, and arts and crafts. A basic pass is $7 and a deluxe pass is $25. Purchase tickets in person at Finley Community Center (2060 W. College Ave.), by phone at 707-543-3737 or online. Howarth Park, 630 Summerfield Road, Santa Rosa, 707-543-3298, srcity.org

Halloweird at El Infierno, Oct. 29

Wine Country event producer and promoter Jake Ward will present his annual, 21-and-over-only Halloweird event — a North Bay Cabaret Halloween variety show — starting at 6 p.m., Oct. 29, at El Infierno Cantina in Santa Rosa. The show will include a cocktail reception with an opening set by DJ Dyops; a variety show featuring comedy, burlesque, pole dancers and drag performances; live music by Oakland swing-punk band Van Goat; and a DJ dance party closing out the night with live visuals, costumed characters and dance beats by DJ Dyops. There will also be a costume contest, live art demos, tarot card readings, a photo booth, two full bars and a kitchen open all night. Costumes encouraged. Tickets range from $25-$315, plus fees. Purchase tickets on Eventbrite. El Infierno Cantina, 120 Fifth St., Santa Rosa. 707-494-6855, northbayevents.com

The Villains Ball at California Theatre, Oct.30

THTR Productions will host a wicked Halloween party from 9 p.m. to 2 a.m., Oct. 30, at The California Theatre. The Villains Ball, hosted by San Francisco drag queen Curveball as Elvira, will include drinks, dancing and drag performances. Guests are encouraged to dress as their favorite villain and compete in the costume contest. Tickets are $30, plus fees. Purchase tickets on Eventbrite. 528 Seventh St., Santa Rosa, 707-664-7529, caltheatre.com

Wine, Witches and Warlocks at Balletto, Oct. 30

Balletto Vineyards will host “Wine, Witches and Warlocks,” a Halloween party and Rotary Club of Sebastopol Sunrise fundraiser, from 5-9 p.m., Oct. 30, at the Santa Rosa estate. The 21-and-over event will include music, dancing, raffle prizes and prizes for best costumes. General admission is $75 and includes two glasses of Balletto wine and hors d’ oeuvres from the Analy High School Culinary Program. All proceeds benefits the Analy culinary program, Dolly Parton’s Imagination Library, The Dogwood Animal Rescue Project and the Redwood Empire Food Bank. Purchase tickets on Eventbrite. Balletto Vineyards, 5700 Occidental Road, Santa Rosa. sebsunriserotary.org

Sonoma

Halloween at The Lodge at Sonoma, Oct. 9

The Lodge at Sonoma will celebrate Halloween with a complimentary outdoor screening of “Beetlejuice” as part of its Movie Night with The Lodge series from 6:30-8:30 p.m., Oct. 9, at The Lodge’s Stone Lawn. The movie starts at 6:45 p.m. and there will be popcorn, beverages and other concessions available for purchase. Guests are encouraged to bring blankets and chairs, as provided seating will be limited. Reserve a spot on Eventbrite. 1325 Broadway, Sonoma, 707-935-6600, thelodgeatsonoma.com

Haunted Wine Country at Sebastiani Theatre, Oct. 16

Petaluma’s Garfield Lane Productions will present its Halloween-themed Haunted Wine Country show at 7 p.m. Oct. 16 at Sebastiani Theatre in Sonoma. The show will include true stories of haunted places around Sonoma, Napa and Mendocino counties, recounted by historians, authors, psychics and paranormal experts. General admission is $17. Purchase tickets online. Sebastiani Theatre, 476 First St. E., Sonoma, 707-996-9756, sebastianitheatre.org

Murder Mystery Magic at Sebastiani Theatre, Oct. 17

The Sebastiani Theatre will host Murder Mystery Magic, a murder-themed one-man magic show, from 7-9 p.m. Oct. 17. The interactive show will include magic and mind-reading demonstrations relating to murderers and criminals. The show is recommended for mature audiences. Tickets are $20; purchase on Eventbrite. 476 First St. E., Sonoma, 707-996-9756, sebastianitheatre.org

Witchie Poo Halloween Extravaganza 2026, Oct. 17, 18, 24, 25

Sebastiani Theatre will present a double weekend production of its annual Witchie Poo Halloween Extravaganza at 1 p.m. on Oct. 17, 18, 24 and 25. Tickets are $11 for children 12 and under and $17 for adults. Purchase tickets online. 476 First St. E., Sonoma, 707-996-9756, sebastianitheatre.org

The Rocky Horror Picture Show at Sebastiani Theater, Oct. 24

Sonoma Valley Pride will present its second annual screening of “The Rocky Horror Picture Show” on Oct. 24 at Sebastiani Theater. title: Sake Brewer Bruce Shimizu Helps Preserve Japanese Culture in Sonoma County
summary:
Bruce Shimizu, a fourth-generation Japanese American, recently opened a sake brewery in Windsor, carrying on his great-grandmother's legacy.

The post Sake Brewer Bruce Shimizu Helps Preserve Japanese Culture in Sonoma County appeared first on Sonoma Magazine.
content:
Bruce Shimizu is doing his part to keep Japanese culture alive in Sonoma County. The 69-year-old Windsor resident is a fourth-generation Japanese American and recently opened a sake brewery in Windsor as a tribute to his great-grandmother, who was sent to an internment camp during World War II.

He has also spearheaded a public Japanese Garden in conjunction with the Japanese American Citizens League (JACL) that’s set to open later this year at Paradise Ridge Winery, a property rich in Japanese American history.

A sake family tradition

My family migrated from Japan to Hawaii in the 1880s and in the 1920s came to Cotati. There was nowhere for them to buy sake unless they went to San Francisco, so my great-grandmother started brewing sake in the basement. The family recipes died with her in the 1950s. A few years ago I was in Sacramento at a brewery and it hit me that sake was something I wanted to do. I’m pretty sure my craft brewery is either the only one or one of a few in the entire country run by American-born Japanese. This is all in addition to the fact that sake is versatile and delicious.

A garden of memories

Before the Byck family bought it, Paradise Ridge was known as Fountaingrove Winery, owned by a man named Kanaye Nagasawa, who was one of the last samurai. The Bycks had one of Nagasawa’s samurai swords on display for years in a little museum; the sword was recovered from the ashes after the Tubbs Fire burned the winery in 2017. Before he died, Walter Byck asked the JACL to help build a garden on the property as a way to acknowledge the past. It is designed to be a place of reflection, inspiration and Zen.

Importance of preserving culture

People don’t know this, but most Japanese Americans in Sonoma County around the time of World War II were rounded up and sent to internment camps in places like Southern Colorado. My family was one of the families that was rounded up. For this reason, it’s important to celebrate this community today. We won’t ever forget the past. At the brewery, we’ll share information about my family’s brewing legacy. At the garden, we’ll have interpretive signage with QR codes that tell guests more about the community. In both places, we just want people to learn.

Shimizu Sake Company, 399 Business Park Court, Suite 521, Windsor, shimizusake.com

title: The Ultimate Guide to Sonoma County Pumpkin Patches in 2026
summary:
Local pumpkin patches offer a variety of fun activities for the whole family, from corn mazes and hay rides to festive seasonal fare and even wine tastings.

The post The Ultimate Guide to Sonoma County Pumpkin Patches in 2026 appeared first on Sonoma Magazine.
content:
The spooky season is here, and pumpkin patches across Sonoma County are welcoming visitors with pumpkins, corn mazes, hayrides, petting zoos, jump zones and other fall attractions. Through October and Halloween, families can pick their own pumpkins, explore seasonal activities and enjoy festive food and treats.

The famed Petaluma Pumpkin Patch on Stony Point Road opened Sept. 25 for its 34th season. Since 1993, locals and visitors have flocked to North Petaluma to find Halloween pumpkins and test their navigation skills in the farm’s 4-acre Amazing Corn Maze, designed by owner and farmer Jim Groverman.

A fourth-generation Sonoma County farmer, Groverman designs a new maze each year, planting more than 150,000 corn seeds to create the course. He also sustainably grows five acres of pumpkins, including more than 50 varieties, as well as other squash.

One of the county’s oldest family-run pumpkin patches, the Petaluma Pumpkin Patch has long been a fall destination for pumpkin picking, corn maze adventures, pony rides and more.

Read on to discover more pumpkin patches across Sonoma County and start planning your 2026 fall outings.

Petaluma

Petaluma Pumpkin Patch

Open Sept. 25 through Oct. 31. The patch features a 4-acre corn maze and a large assortment of pumpkins to pick, making it a popular autumn destination. It also has local food vendors and children’s activities like pony rides, jump houses, face painting and a carnival fun slide. Open 10 a.m. to 7 p.m. Sunday through Thursday and 10 a.m. to 10 p.m. Friday and Saturday. General admission is free; tickets for attractions range from $3 to $13. 450 Stony Point Road, Petaluma, 707-781-3132, petalumapumpkinpatch.com

Mickelson Pumpkin Patch

Open Sept. 19 through Nov. 8. The patch offers a wide variety of traditional and specialty pumpkins for sale from 9 a.m. to 8 p.m. Sunday through Thursday, and from 9 a.m. to 10 p.m. Friday and Saturday. Open on Halloween, Oct. 31, from 9 a.m. to 6 p.m. Activities include cornhole, giant Jenga, an apple cannon, paintball gallery, corn pits, a 1-acre hay maze, grain train rides, a super slide and a jump zone. Admission rangea from free to $30. Food vendors are also on site. 5495 Redwood Highway South, Petaluma, 707-490-8088, mickelsonpumpkinpatch.com

Pronzini Farms Pumpkin Patch

Open Sept. 26 through Oct. 31. The patch offers a variety of pumpkins in a rural setting with decorated vintage vehicles. Attractions include a haunted trail and western village, hay tower, giant slides, bounce houses, tractor rides, petting zoo, steer toss and corn pit. Local food vendors include Petaluma’s Sax’s Joint and Tacos Don Pepe, and Santa Rosa’s El Brinquito. Live music plays from noon to 5:30 p.m. Saturday and Sunday. Admission ranges from free to $10, with many activities included. Punch cards for premium attractions range from $33 to $110. In October, the patch hosts guided tours through the haunted village from 7-10 p.m. Fridays and Saturdays. Fright Night tickets are $25 and recommended for ages 12 and over. Hours are 11 a.m. to 7 p.m. Monday through Thursday and 10 a.m. to 7 p.m. Friday through Sunday. 3795 Adobe Road, Petaluma, 707-778-3871, pronzinifarms.com

Pumpkins on Pikes

Tara Firma Farms will present its magical Pumpkins on Pikes fundraiser from 2-9 p.m. on Oct. 17, 24 and 25. Participants can pick a pumpkin to carve and decorate on site, then mount their lit jack-o’-lanterns on pikes for a Halloween display. Food, drinks, live music and games will be available. Tickets are $40 and include one pumpkin. Children 3 and under attend free. Purchase tickets online. 3796 I St., Petaluma, 707-765-1202, tarafirmafarms.com

Santa Rosa

Santa Rosa Pumpkin Patch

Open Sept. 26 through Oct. 31. The patch offers a wide range of activities and a variety of pumpkins for sale. Attractions include a Barnyard Ballzone, an 8-acre corn maze, a hay bale pyramid, petting zoo, bounce houses, cornhole, pony rides, pumpkin tic-tac-toe and apple blasters. General admission is $5 and includes access to several activities. Passes for premium activities, including the corn maze, range from $12 to $30. Pumpkins are priced by size. Admission is free for children 2 and under. Open 11 a.m. to 7 p.m. Monday through Thursday; 11 a.m. to 9 p.m. Friday; 9 a.m. to 9 p.m. Saturday; and 9 a.m. to 8 p.m. Sunday. The patch closes at 6 p.m. sharp on Oct. 31. 5157 Stony Point Road, Santa Rosa, 707-582-3276, santarosapumpkinpatch.com

Muelrath Ranches Pumpkin Patch

Open Sept. 26 through Oct. 31. The patch offers free family activities with the purchase of a pumpkin. It includes a haunted house, picnic area, hay pyramid, toddler’s corn maze and narrated hay ride. Refreshments are available for purchase. Antique tractors from the Santa Rosa branch of the National Early Day Gas Engine and Tractor Association will be on display from 2-5:30 p.m. Oct. 17-18. Open 10 a.m. to 6 p.m. daily. 3800 Walker Ave., Santa Rosa. 707-585-2195, muelrathspumpkins.com

Punky’s Pumpkins

Open Oct. 1 through Oct. 31. Punky’s has been a reliable hometown pumpkin patch since 1995, offering a wide selection of pumpkins and other squash. Attractions include Johnny Popper tractor hay rides, train rides, bounce houses, a giant slide, a disco corn pit and cartoon billboards for photo ops. Snow cones, cotton candy and fresh-squeezed lemonade are available on weekends. Bring a lunch to enjoy at the picnic tables. Open 11 a.m. to 9 p.m. Monday through Friday and 9 a.m. to 9 p.m. Saturday and Sunday. Admission is free; tickets for select attractions range from $2 to $5; wristbands for all-day unlimited access are $25. 50 Mark West Springs Road, Santa Rosa, 707-579-8474, punkysadobefarm.com 

Floating Pumpkin Patch

The Ridgway Swim Center will host its 15th annual Floating Pumpkin Patch on Oct. 17, with three two-hour sessions (starting at 10 a.m., 1:30 p.m. and 3:45 p.m.). Participants can pick a bobbing pumpkin from the pool and decorate it at the decorating station. Other games, crafts and prizes will be available all afternoon. Entry fee is $16 (pumpkin included); children under 2 enter free. 455 Ridgway Ave., Santa Rosa, 707-543-3421, srcity.org

Sonoma

Larson Family Winery’s Pumpkin Patch

Open throughout October. Enjoy family-friendly fall activities alongside wine tasting for adults. The patch is free to roam, with pumpkins and gourds available for purchase. The winery will host a canine costume contest from 11 a.m. to 1 p.m. Oct. 25, with wine-related prizes for the top three costumed pups. Tickets are $5 for children and $20 per adult, including a glass of wine. Cornhole reservations are $40 and include bottle service. Purchase tickets on Tock. 23355 Millerick Road, Sonoma, 707-938-3031, larsonfamilywinery.com

Healdsburg

Orsi Family Vineyards Pumpkin Patch

This Healdsburg winery will host a Pumpkins & Pizza Pick-Up Party from noon to 3 p.m. Oct. 24. The fall party will include live music, wine, small bites, wood-fired pizza and pumpkins to take home. Free for wine club members and $25 for non-members. Reserve a spot on Tock. 2306 Magnolia Drive, Healdsburg, 707-732-4660, orsifamilyvineyards.com

Grandma’s Pumpkin Patch

Open Sept. 26 through Oct. 31. Enjoy an old-fashioned experience where guests can purchase locally grown pumpkins and take part in classic fall activities. The patch includes vintage tractors, a hay pyramid, baby animals and macaroni necklace-making. Class field trips are $7 per student. The patch is ADA-compliant. Open from 10 a.m. to dusk daily. 17740 Healdsburg Ave., Healdsburg, 707-293-5750, facebook.com/HealdsburgGranny

title: Gold Ridge Organic Farms Releases New Collection of Artful Olive Oils
summary:
Gold Ridge Organic Farms in Sebastopol recently introduced its most colorful collection of extra-virgin olive oils yet.

The post Gold Ridge Organic Farms Releases New Collection of Artful Olive Oils appeared first on Sonoma Magazine.
content:
Gold Ridge Organic Farms founder Brooke Hazen laughs when asked if he’s ever personally counted the 13,000 olive trees he claims to have when he leads tours around his hillside Sebastopol ranch. It’s a precise number, but completely believable for the meticulously groomed 70-acre orchard planted in a diverse selection of Italian, Spanish and French cultivars. He is positive, he quips, that his team harvests “more than 20” varieties each fall, and the result is “a lot, a lot” of premium olives.

This summer, Hazen introduced a collection of With Love from Sonoma County extra-virgin olive oils that showcases his deep love of the fruit, and also another passion: art.

A self-described “Earth Artist,” he nurtures his farm — a rich 18-acre tapestry of heirloom apples, citrus and pears thrives here, too — and works collaboratively with renowned local artists to create large-scale, interactive pieces for his property. Stroll the grounds, and you’ll see playful sculptures from Sebastopol’s famous junk repurposer Patrick Amiot, agricultural-themed murals, and even art you can ride in via an adorable trolley embossed with oversized flowers, fruit, and furry critters that’s used for farm tours and in the annual Apple Blossom Parade.

For this new release, Hazen partnered with Sonoma County artist Teri Sloat and her daughter, Carrie Dufour, creative director of Petaluma-based Truly Creative, to design boldly colored bottles with labels featuring Sloat’s artwork. Each variety of oil has a unique label design.

“We share a belief in the emotional power of color, joy, energy and a sense of celebration,” Sloat says. “Each label is designed to evoke the qualities and flavors inside the bottle, to enliven the space around it, and bring warmth and beauty to the table where it rests.”

Using olives that are milled on-site in a state-of-the-art press within hours of harvest to preserve quality and flavor, Gold Ridge Organic Farms produces four organic extra-virgin olive oils, including an herbaceous Tuscan blend; a toasty, peppery Minerva blend; a bold, spicy French Picholine blend; and an Arbequina blend that hints of tropical fruit and green peppercorn. The farm’s citrus trees inspire other flavors, including oils infused with Meyer lemon, mandarin-kumquat, yuzu citrus, makrut lime and blood orange.

More than just a pretty package, the oils have earned top marks from judges, racking up gold, double gold, and best of class awards from a number of recent international competitions, the California State Fair and the Sonoma County Harvest Fair.

Gold Ridge Organic Farms, 3387 Canfield Road, Sebastopol. 707-823-3110, goldridgeorganicfarms.com

title: Where to Get the Best Steak in Sonoma County
summary:
Finding steak on a menu isn't hard. Finding a great steak, however, is a quest. We've found the best in Sonoma County.

The post Where to Get the Best Steak in Sonoma County appeared first on Sonoma Magazine.
content:
Finding steak on a restaurant menu isn’t hard. Finding a really great one can feel like a quest.

Steak is deceptively simple. It doesn’t need a moat of sauce, a dusting of charcoal salt or a thicket of tweezered garnishes. The best versions come down to beef, salt, heat and someone who knows exactly when to leave the meat alone.

So why pay restaurant prices for something you can grill at home? Because great steak is about more than putting a piece of beef over a fire. It’s about sourcing, aging and technique. Restaurants have access to exceptional cuts, locally raised beef and prized Wagyu, while chefs know how to coax a deeply browned crust from the meat without turning its rosy center into expensive shoe leather.

And please: Don’t order it well-done. It’s a travesty.

Here are some of our favorite steaks in Sonoma County, from Wagyu splurges and hulking rib-eyes to straightforward steak frites that can be justified on a Tuesday.

Best of the Best

Journeyman Meat Co.: Part butcher shop, part cafe, Journeyman lets you choose your cut from the meat case and have the kitchen cook it in its wood-fired oven. These aren’t ordinary grocery-store steaks. We’re talking prime cuts, including Australian Wagyu with enough marbling to resemble an Italian palazzo. For a thrifty $30, order the 5-ounce butcher’s-choice steak with salad. It may be the best steak you’ll find in Healdsburg. 404 Center St., Healdsburg, 707-395-6328, journeymanmeat.com

Stark’s Steak & Seafood: Go for happy hour, stay for the steak. The menu is unapologetically beef-centric: dry-aged, hickory-smoked, topped with roasted bone marrow or wrapped in bacon. The sides deserve attention, too, especially the house-baked rolls with garlic butter, creamed spinach and creme fraiche mashed potatoes. 521 Adams St., Santa Rosa, 707-546-5100, starkssteakhouse.com

Seared: This downtown steakhouse is a local favorite, known as much for its happy-hour deals as for its lobster mac and cheese and beefy rib-eyes. Prime cuts run from $46 to $65, including sides, while a 42-ounce tomahawk steak with prawns and bone marrow butter is $130. It isn’t cheap, but at least you won’t be gouged for every side dish or upsold on sea salt harvested by mermaids. 170 Petaluma Blvd. N., Petaluma, 707-762-5997, petalumaseared.com

Stockhome: Steak frites gets the Scandinavian-by-way-of-France treatment at this Petaluma favorite. An 8-ounce grilled filet comes with salad, crisp pommes frites and bearnaise, the buttery tarragon sauce that exists largely to remind us that steak and butter make excellent companions. 220 Western Ave., Petaluma, 707-981-8511, stockhomepetaluma.com

Underwood Bar & Bistro: Sometimes you don’t need Wagyu genealogy or a hand-honed steak knife. Underwood is about the simple pleasures, like flat iron steak with a pile of fries. You’re in the right place. 9113 Graton Road, Graton, 707-823-7023, underwoodgraton.com

Songbird Parlour: Songbird goes big with a 16-ounce prime rib-eye crusted in earthy Urfa chile. Wednesday brings prime rib night, with herb-crusted cuts served with jus and fresh horseradish. Come hungry, or bring someone willing to share. 14301 Arnold Drive, Suite 3, Glen Ellen, 707-343-1308, songbirdparlour.com

AYA: Chef Roy Ellamar’s rooftop restaurant at Graton Resort & Casino has built an entire Wagyu program around beef from Japan, Australia and the United States. There’s wood-grilled Akaushi rib-eye, Mishima Ranch coulotte and a Wagyu flight for anyone unable to commit to a single cut. 288 Golf Course Drive W. at Graton Resort & Casino, Rohnert Park, 707-588-3750, ayasonoma.com

Guiso Latin Fusion: Chimichurri, blistered shishito peppers and spicy mustard greens bring heat and brightness to a simple hanger steak. Chef Carlos Mojica’s cooking draws on Latin, Caribbean and South American flavors, with the kind of spice and storytelling that make the dish memorable. 117 North St., Healdsburg, 707-431-1302, guisolatinfusion.com

Bijou: This elegant take on the French bistro classic restored my faith after one too many encounters with gristly, undercooked hanger steak and gloopy bordelaise. At Bijou, generous slices of tender steak arrive with a lush peppercorn sauce and fries neatly parked alongside, crisp and ready for dunking. 190 Kentucky St., Petaluma, 707-753-9155, restaurantbijou.com

Valette: American Kobe beef tartare with truffles and egg-yolk emulsion is one of Dustin Valette’s signatures. His prime New York strip loin is the more substantial indulgence, served with a potato croquette, bone marrow, Périgord truffle butter and sauce bordelaise. There are steaks, and then there are steaks that arrive with bone marrow and truffles. 344 Center St., Healdsburg, 707-473-0946, valettehealdsburg.com

Wit & Wisdom: Chef Michael Mina’s Sonoma restaurant gives steak the wood-fire treatment. The lineup includes a 12-ounce prime New York strip, an 8-ounce center-cut filet mignon and a 16-ounce prime rib-eye, all served with red-wine demi-glace. Add blue-cheese crust, chimichurri or creamy horseradish if you feel compelled to gild the beefy lily. Wednesday’s Wagyu special brings a wood-grilled Westholme flat iron with sauce au poivre, truffle butter and truffle fries. 1325 Broadway, Sonoma, 707-931-3410, witandwisdomsonoma.com

Goodnight’s Prime Steak + Spirits: Backed by wine mogul and entrepreneur Bill Foley, Goodnight’s makes no attempt to disguise what it is: a tufted-leather-banquette, beef-centric cowboy fantasy for the well-heeled. The prices reflect that. But if you’re after a hefty tomahawk or a 32-ounce dry-aged porterhouse in a tony Healdsburg setting, this is the place. 113 Plaza St., Healdsburg, 707-543-1000, goodnightsrestaurant.com

More Great Steaks

Santa Rosa

Monti’s: Monti’s keeps things relaxed with grilled Certified Angus Beef flat iron steak, royal trumpet mushrooms, mustard and tarragon butter. It’s the kind of steak dinner that feels indulgent without requiring a birthday, anniversary or expense account. 714 Village Court, Santa Rosa, 707-568-4404, montismv.com

Kenwood

Salt & Stone: Steak is a staple at this picturesque Kenwood restaurant, with rib-eye, filet mignon and bavette among the choices. You can take the filet in “Salt & Stone” fashion with roasted lobster tail, sautéed Gulf prawns or seared scallops. Buttermilk mashed Yukon Gold potatoes, blue-cheese demi-glace, Cabernet butter and wine salt make clear that this is not spa food. 9900 Sonoma Highway, Kenwood, 707-833-6326, saltstonekenwood.com

Glen Ellen

Glen Ellen Star: The wood-fired oven is the heart of this tiny-but-mighty Sonoma Valley restaurant, and meat coming out of it tends to get our attention. Chef Ari Weiswasser’s Wagyu Denver steak comes with chanterelle mushrooms, roasted sunchokes and peppercorn cream sauce. 13648 Arnold Drive, Glen Ellen, 707-343-1384, glenellenstar.com

Sonoma

El Dorado Kitchen: The courtyard alone can make dinner feel like an occasion. The filet mignon seals the deal, served with roasted Yukon Gold potatoes, king trumpet mushrooms, cauliflower, bordelaise and truffle purée. Add the truffle-Parmesan fries if restraint has already left the building. 405 First St. W., Sonoma, 707-996-3030, eldoradosonoma.com

Sonoma Grille: Surf and turf is alive and well here. Order the filet mignon, then add half a Maine lobster because apparently regular dinner wasn’t extravagant enough. It comes with sautéed green beans, cremini mushrooms, blue-cheese herb butter and roasted pearl-onion sauce. 165 W. Napa St., Sonoma, 707-938-7542, sonomagrilleandbar.com

Petaluma

Stormy’s Spirits & Supper: Established as a roadhouse in 1854, Stormy’s became a steakhouse in the early 1970s and remains gloriously old-school. Prime rib is the move, and the prices are especially appealing when you consider that dinner includes housemade clam chowder, salad, mashed potatoes, vegetables and French bread. Nobody leaves wondering where the rest of the meal went. 6650 Bloomfield Road, Petaluma, 707-795-0127, stormysrestaurant.com

Rohnert Park

Cattlemens: This is the traditional Western steakhouse version of dinner, complete with ranch-style surroundings, hand-cut beef and enough prime rib options to require a minor consultation. Cuts come in 9, 12 and 16 ounces, while “beef and reef” combinations pair steak with seafood. 4619 Redwood Drive, Rohnert Park, 707-585-7603, cattlemens.com

630 Park Steakhouse: Here’s your big-time casino steakhouse, where the cuts are serious, the sides are rich and caviar is considered a perfectly reasonable companion to a large piece of beef. This is not the night for sensible choices. Graton Resort & Casino, 288 Golf Course Drive W., Rohnert Park, 707-588-7115, graton.com

Healdsburg

Hazel Hill: Montage Healdsburg’s signature restaurant brings French technique and Wine Country polish to the steak dinner. An 8-ounce bavette with sauce au poivre delivers the classic peppery, creamy combination, with vineyard views thrown in for good measure. 100 Montage Way, Healdsburg, 707-979-9000, montage.com

title: Pick Your Own Steak for Lunch at Journeyman Meat Co. in Healdsburg
summary:
At Pete Seghesio's butcher shop, $30 buys a wood-fired prime steak, a big salad and garlic bread, plus some of the best salumi in Sonoma County.

The post Pick Your Own Steak for Lunch at Journeyman Meat Co. in Healdsburg appeared first on Sonoma Magazine.
content:
In Healdsburg, $30 will get you one and a half fancy cocktails, a couple of burritos or one of the best steak lunches you’ve ever had. You just have to know where to go.

For the steak, go to Journeyman Meat Co., a butcher shop speakeasy owned by Pete and Cathy Seghesio. Yes, those Seghesios: the family behind Seghesio Family Vineyards, one of Sonoma County’s oldest wineries.

From the sidewalk, Journeyman looks like a meat market. Long refrigerated cases hold sausages and brown-paper-wrapped cuts. There’s a busy meat counter, a very expensive Italian meat slicer and, most days, plenty of locals.

Journeyman is Pete Seghesio’s longtime passion project, where he carries on a family tradition of making fresh sausages and premium salumi while selling some seriously high-end beef: perfectly marbled Wagyu and Angus cattle raised by his son, Will, for the company’s estate program.

It’s the kind of beef that can cost $200 at a restaurant.

But regulars know you can also eat at Journeyman. Inside the long, narrow shop are a handful of cozy tables, with a few more outside in the alley. Friends of Pete’s — and club members — can sit at the marble counter, sip a glass of wine and wait for a 5-ounce premium steak cooked to order in the wood-fired oven.

For $30, the steak comes on a wooden board with a giant pile of salad and garlic bread. The “butcher’s cut,” selected by the shop, is the value option. You can also upgrade to any cut in the case.

It might be one of the best steaks you’ve had. It will almost certainly be one of the better deals you’ll find in Healdsburg.

But the steak is only part of the story.

Salumi and sausage

Journeyman is a second act for Seghesio. After years as the winery’s chief executive, he decided to pursue artisan sausage and salumi, carrying on a tradition his grandparents brought with them from Northern Italy.

He spent five winters studying whole-animal butchery and curing with Dario Cecchini in Panzano and the Marini family in Florence before returning home to build Journeyman.

In 2016, he opened a 12,000-square-foot, USDA-certified production facility in Cloverdale to make the charcuterie and sausage that put Journeyman on the map. Unlike mass-market salumi, which can be hurried along with heat, Seghesio’s 6-ounce logs, known as chubs, can take 38 days or more to cure.

The slower process produces a noticeably different flavor, Seghesio explained — less aggressively tangy, more sweet and savory.

Journeyman’s flagship Pio salumi is based on his grandmother’s recipe, seasoned with nutmeg, clove, garlic and white wine. Wine is treated almost like another seasoning, generally making up about 1% of a recipe — roughly the same amount as garlic.

A salumi board might include soppressata; fennel-forward finocchiona; spicy ’nduja; Holy Mole, made with Mexican mole spices; Volo, with chocolate, Napa Valley cherries and nuts; and Rosso, layered with juniper, anise, mustard and whole spices.

The wood-fired pizzas, made on-site, are essentially delivery systems for cured meats.

In short: go for the steak, stay for the pizza and come back for the burger — and, if you’re lucky, the secret Sunday Cubano. Journeyman is a local butcher shop that happens to be much more than rib-eyes and sausages.

Best bets

Journeyman’s Estate Bacon Burger, $17: This burger is one of the better things to come out of the 2017 wildfires. During the fires, when buying a fancy steak was understandably low on many people’s lists, sales dropped sharply. Seghesio had a case full of prime meat with a short shelf life, so he pivoted: He ground it into burgers. The idea stuck. Today’s burger is made with prime chuck mixed with about 15% Journeyman bacon and the shop’s house spice blend, then tucked into a rosemary bun. I don’t want to over gush, but it’s so good I’ve considered proposing.

Butcher’s steak, $30: A 5-ounce prime-or-better steak with garlic bread and a generous salad. Upgrade if something in the case catches your eye.

Salumi board, $38: The best introduction to what Journeyman does. The selections change, but a butcher’s board piled with six types of thinly sliced artisan salumi, cheese and pickles makes a solid afternoon snack for two.

Pizza, $22: The pepperoni is lovely, but the DooJa, made with Journeyman’s house ’nduja, is next-level. The spicy, spreadable salumi — a favorite among chefs — tops a white pizza with smoked mozzarella and leeks. There’s also the Rosso, with sausage, peppers and taleggio, and the Bianco, with Cowgirl Creamery’s Wagon Wheel cheese, bacon and a sunny-side-up egg in the middle. The Wagon Wheel was originally made for Zuni Cafe’s pizzas.

BLT, $17: It’s famous for a reason. Journeyman makes the bacon used at three-Michelin-starred SingleThread, which is kind of a big deal. The bacon is tumbled and cured, then cut into meaty slices and served on sourdough with heirloom tomato, lettuce and mayonnaise.

Daily specials: Wednesday is cheesesteak day, Friday is meatball day and Sunday is all about the Cubano.

Journeyman doesn’t take reservations for regular dining, and the small room fills quickly on busy weekends.

The spot

It’s a long story, but the stately building that houses SingleThread restaurant and inn was originally supposed to be Seghesio’s sausage and cured-meat factory. It all worked out for the best, and Journeyman carved out a small nook for itself in the Center Street building. So, if nothing else, you can say you’ve eaten next door to SingleThread.

Journeyman Meat Co. is open 11 a.m. to 7 p.m. Wednesday through Sunday and 10 a.m. to 5 p.m. Monday, with a limited menu on Mondays. Closed Tuesday. 404 Center St., Healdsburg; 707-395-MEAT, journeymanmeat.com

title: Bigger Kitchen, More Brunch: Wild Poppy Cafe Expands at The Barlow in Sebastopol
summary:
After building a following at their cozy west Sebastopol cafe, Martin and Danielle Maigaard have opened a larger restaurant and marketplace with sunny patio dining, brunch favorites and room to bake.

The post Bigger Kitchen, More Brunch: Wild Poppy Cafe Expands at The Barlow in Sebastopol appeared first on Sonoma Magazine.
content:
For 22 years, Martin and Danielle Maigaard dreamed of opening a restaurant with a spacious kitchen, room to bake, ample parking and an artisan marketplace bigger than a closet.

Instead, in 2024, they fell for a quirky-cool roadhouse in west Sebastopol that had none of those things. Wild Poppy Cafe, at 9890 Bodega Highway, was small, a little out of the way and simply too charming to resist.

“We wanted to start small and make sure it was received well,” Martin said.

It was. The cafe became a rarity in the restaurant business: a runaway success. Perhaps it was the quiet creekside patio, the fresh pastries or the beans and greens that became a signature dish. (This is west county, after all.)

Still, the couple dreamed of a little more space — especially in the kitchen and the parking lot.

Their new Wild Poppy Cafe and Marketplace at The Barlow delivers on both counts. Open for just a few weeks, the 3,500-square-foot former brewery has been drawing crowds for brunch and lunch, with diners settling onto the sunny patio over Korean chicken rice bowls, tacos and French toast topped with apple compote.

The Barlow is hardly short on good food and drink. Sarmentine turns out pastries, Taylor Lane serves coffee, and Acre Pizza, Sushi Kosho and Genero’s offer plenty of dining options. But Wild Poppy fills a different niche: a relaxed, brunch-friendly gathering place for Wednesday morning meetups, work-from-home days when you don’t actually want to work from home, and leisurely weekend meals.

“You walk in and it feels like home,” Martin said. “We wanted it to feel like we were hosting, like a backyard gathering or a dinner party.”

Danielle was quick to add another ingredient to the formula.

“And everyone we hire has to be nice. Customers see that, and I think that’s really helped us along.”

A new location, a familiar menu

Opening a second restaurant was no walk in the park. It was more like six months of welding torches and saws.

Martin, who has spent years renovating homes, handled much of the construction himself at the original cafe on Bodega Highway. At The Barlow, he took the same do-it-yourself approach, working without a contractor. The project took longer than expected, but the savings made the extra effort worthwhile.

The new cafe retains customer favorites, including Baja fish tacos and Cosmic Queso nachos, while adding a handful of dishes: fancy toast, salads, a salmon burger and rice bowls.

The marketplace brings together local products and fair-trade goods, including pottery, spices, blankets, napkins, towels and Wild Poppy merchandise. A deli case is being stocked with grab-and-go soups, dips and salads.

Coffee and espresso drinks share the menu with beer, wine and a sunny turmeric lemonade made in-house. Save room for the housemade gluten-free peanut butter chocolate chip cookies.

Restaurant success stories have become harder to come by. But the Maigaards appear to have found a formula that works in west Sonoma County.

That’s something worth raising a mimosa to.

Details: Wild Poppy Cafe & Market is at 6780 McKinley St., Suite 160, Sebastopol. Open 10 a.m. to 3 p.m. Wednesday through Monday and closed Tuesday.

Wild Poppy Creekside is at 9890 Bodega Highway, Sebastopol. Open 10 a.m. to 3 p.m. Thursday through Sunday. thewildpoppycafe.com

title: We Had Breakfast With Sonoma County’s Smashburger King
summary:
Smashburger maestro Justin Haley and dining editor Heather Irwin meet for breakfast, talking about food, life, love and favorite restaurants.

The post We Had Breakfast With Sonoma County’s Smashburger King appeared first on Sonoma Magazine.
content:
Justin Haley is Sonoma County’s king of smashburgers. Not all kings wear crowns. Some wear T-shirts and chef’s pants.

You’ll usually find Haley, a gentle giant, working the flattop beneath a black pop-up tent at breweries, farmers markets and local events, turning out the thin burgers he’s perfected over the years, with crunchy cheese and char around the edges. But the real draw is the neon-orange sauce that squeezes out from every crevice.

It’s not quite Thousand Island dressing, and it’s not quite barbecue sauce. Rich with spices and a hint of smoke, it’s something entirely its own. Haley won’t tell you the recipe, but he will tell you the inspiration.

“I wanted something alarmingly orange colored,” he said. “My goal was the Nickelodeon orange. But with no dyes. I wanted that nostalgic color. And it needed to pair well with wine and beer — we’re in Sonoma County after all.”

Haley also loves working the register and holding court with customers. Children are particularly fascinated by the sauce’s improbable hue, and he often goes home with their drawings.

He’s equally generous with his fellow food vendors, sharing spare napkins, giving away burgers and lending an extra set of hands when someone is in the weeds, even during a heated food competition. He usually wins anyway. That’s just the kind of guy Haley is.

After a busy weekend of events and another People’s Choice Award, this time at the Smash Bash smashburger showdown at Shady Oak Barrel House, we met for breakfast at one of his favorite spots, Marvin’s of Cotati, to talk burgers, breakfast and the pleasures of cooking in Sonoma County.

Let’s meet for breakfast

Even on a Tuesday morning, Marvin’s is packed. Tucked into a quiet strip mall, it’s the kind of place you might drive past without a second thought. Locals know better.

The restaurant is a destination for hearty steak and eggs, pancakes and its specialty, chilaquiles: crisp tortilla chips piled with eggs, chorizo and a deep-brown mole, a smoky, slightly sweet chile sauce made in-house.

Over two generous plates of chilaquiles that threaten to overpower both our appetite and our resolve, Haley and I dig in.

First off, where did the name Thanks for the Invite come from?

My wife, Paige, and I spent months traveling across California looking for the perfect burger. We tried everything. Big cities, small towns, roadside stops. We paid attention and started to notice what made certain burgers stand out and why others were easy to forget. It was not about doing the most. It was about doing it right.

We practiced a lot back home, trying to get our own burger just right, and then invited friends over to try them. Everyone loved them and ended up saying, “Thanks for the invite!”

Why did you pick Marvin’s for our breakfast?

It’s a classic breakfast staple. They aren’t trying to do anything crazy. From the jams and jellies to salsa and mole, everything is made in-house by the family, something you don’t see much anymore.

What does breakfast look like for you on a normal day?

I don’t eat breakfast. It’s rare, but when I do, I like to kinda go all out and order pancakes to share for the table. Every time.

What’s better: Tacos or burritos?

I love them both, but I’m a nacho guy at heart. When I was 11 years old, I used to write nacho reviews. The old Rafa’s in Cotati used to bake enchilada sauce into their chips and cheese, and I think about that pretty often.

What’s something you love about cooking in Sonoma County?

The people! I feel like Sonoma County’s food community is actually massive. Whenever I have a weird idea, I know there’s always somebody nearby who’s going to try it. I feel like the community supports locals so much, something you can’t really find in a big city.

What are you obsessed with right now, food or otherwise?

Salads. I don’t look like it, but I’m a sucker for a salad. Also, my wife, Paige.

What’s your favorite restaurant or chef in Sonoma County?

Diavola. They just do everything so absolutely right, and at a price point you can’t beat. I’m a huge fan of sharing plates, and I think that’s just a perfect spot to do it. Also, the Gun Club (same owners) has our favorite smashburger (besides our own).

What would you eat for your last meal? Because I think this Mexican hot chocolate from Marvin’s is on my list.

I’d love some toasted sourdough bread, butter with a little extra salt, a little local honey, and some ripe peaches and pluots under a tree in a field in Sonoma County with the love of my life.

What food trends do you hate?

Height on food. Like, I don’t want a tall sandwich or tall burger. Flatten that thing out and make it wider. My mouth can’t open that much!

Who should I interview next?

Beryl Adler of Acorn Cafe in Healdsburg. That guy is magic, and he’s a massive inspiration.

Details about where to find Justin and Thanks for the Invite can be found at instagram.com/thanksfortheinvite.ca.

title: From Fries to Fine Dining: The Greek at Appellation Healdsburg
summary:
Food truck chef Dino Moniodis trades gyros and fries for five-course Greek dinners at Folia in Healdsburg, showing off his fine-dining chops.

The post From Fries to Fine Dining: The Greek at Appellation Healdsburg appeared first on Sonoma Magazine.
content:
Dino Moniodis can turn out a mean lamb gyro, falafel plate and seasoned fries from the tiny kitchen of his Greek food truck. Give him a state-of-the-art kitchen, a live-fire grill and room to experiment, though, and the 34-year-old chef is in his element.

After years of cooking Greek street food, Moniodis is getting a chance to showcase his fine-dining skills at Folia Bar + Kitchen in Healdsburg, trading takeout containers for five-course dinners.

“It’s pretty amazing,” he said as he prepared for his Monday night dinner series, The Greek at Appellation Healdsburg.

The pop-up series began in late September and has sold out every week, Moniodis said. The $85 dinner begins with family-style mezze, including phyllo-wrapped feta drizzled with honey, roasted tomatoes, kataifi-wrapped prawns and tender octopus.

“It’s the way a Greek table actually works,” he said.

A family tradition of cooking

Moniodis spent much of his childhood summers on the Greek island of Chios, working at his family’s taverna. Sharing food around the table was tradition, and it remains central to how he wants guests to experience his cooking.

The main course might be a wood-fired pork or lamb chop, depending on the week, accompanied by roasted eggplant, lentils and a charred apple-and-lemon beurre blanc. It’s good enough to make sharing feel like an unreasonable demand — I guarded my plate from wandering forks and used a piece of leftover pita to mop up the last of the sauce.

It’s the kind of cooking Moniodis rarely gets to do in his 10-by-10-foot food truck kitchen, where elaborate plating and more ambitious techniques are hard to pull off. Trained in kitchens across Sonoma County, including several years at Willi’s Wine Bar, he’s got the chops, classic sauces and knife skills down. What he has lacked is the space and opportunity to spread his wings.

“I’ve had the training, but not the platform,” he said.

Greek food is personal

Moniodis’ summers in Greece remain a touchstone, a mix of playing on the beach with cousins and learning to cook at the taverna. Later, while caring for his father during a serious illness, the two discussed opening a Greek restaurant.

After his father’s death in 2018, Moniodis decided to pursue that dream. He launched Dino’s Greek Food in 2019.

The business led to other ventures, including Zimi on Mission in Santa Rosa, where he paired Greek staples like spanakopita, dolmas and pastitsio with wood-fired pizzas. The restaurant closed after 18 months, but Moniodis was not ready to abandon the restaurant he and his father had envisioned.

An opportunity to move closer to that goal came in April, when Moniodis was named one of the North Bay Business Journal’s 40 Under 40. At the awards event, he met chef Charlie Palmer and his sons, Reed and Courtland, who are involved with Appellation Healdsburg, a culinary-focused resort that opened in September 2025. Reed leads the kitchen at Folia Bar + Kitchen, while Courtland is president of Appellation. The resort is also home to Andys Beeline Rooftop Bar.

Moniodis introduced himself and pitched an idea: a Monday night series devoted to Greek cooking at Folia. The Palmers agreed, and The Greek debuted in September. Charlie Palmer has confirmed that the series will continue into the fall.

“He’s been very lenient, just letting me do whatever I want to do,” Moniodis said.

The arrangement has offered more than a chance to cook. Moniodis has also gained a closer look at the business of fine dining, from menu development and staffing to marketing and reservations. Unlike running his own kitchens, he now has an established team to rely on.

“It feels like I’m running a small restaurant,” he said. “It’s nice to be part of a team and lean on people and get back into the kitchen.”

For now, Moniodis is cooking the food he loves in the setting he has long wanted. Each Monday brings him a little closer to the Greek restaurant he and his father dreamed of opening. One dinner at a time.

Details: The Greek at Appellation offers five-course dinners for $85 per person, with Greek wines available separately. Reservations are available through OpenTable. 101 Dovetail Lane, Healdsburg, 707-723-2130, foliabarandkitchen.com

title: Inside J&M’s Midtown Cafe, a Santa Rosa Breakfast Favorite
summary:
At J&M’s Midtown Cafe, longtime chef Joel Shaw puts his own spin on a beloved Santa Rosa breakfast spot without messing with the dishes regulars love.

The post Inside J&M’s Midtown Cafe, a Santa Rosa Breakfast Favorite appeared first on Sonoma Magazine.
content:
When Joel and Marla Shaw bought Dierk’s Midtown Cafe in 2023, they knew better than to tamper with crowd favorites like smoked salmon hash, Gompa’s pancake breakfast and the beloved Country Benedict.

Joel Shaw had been one of those regulars before he became the owner. A longtime chef and devoted breakfast fan, he and Marla understood how much the neighborhood loved the restaurant, founded by chef Mark Dierkhising, who also opened Dierk’s Parkside Cafe.

Still, even a classic can stand a little reinvention.

Keeping the best of the past with an eye toward the future, the couple created J&M’s Midtown Cafe. For Joel, a former cook at Ramen Gaijin in Sebastopol, the kitchen became a kind of laboratory, a place to experiment with ingredients and techniques without losing sight of what brought customers through the door.

He raised the bar on the New York-style pastrami sandwich by brining the meat in-house and added one of his own diner favorites, chicken-fried steak. Seasonal hashes offer another outlet for his creativity. Recently, he worked pickled grapes into a hash, using fruit from the restaurant’s back porch. Inspired by Persian cuisine, he has his eye on pomegranates, which he’s considering adding to a duck confit.

But there’s a limit to how much he wants to change — he knows when to let a good thing be.

The cafe has been a dream come true for Joel, which made the illness that sidelined him a year ago all the more difficult. He could not lift a saucepan, let alone wash dishes or bus tables, and faced a long recovery.

The staff kept the restaurant going. Bussers picked up shifts, kitchen workers came in on their days off, and Marla and the couple’s son filled in wherever they were needed. Their efforts carried the cafe through until Joel could return to work.

Now he’s back to doing a little of everything: cooking, taking orders, clearing tables and washing dishes when the cafe gets busy, which happens often enough because regulars keep arriving for their pancake breakfasts and Benedicts.

The details

How long in business: The location has been a breakfast and brunch destination for more than a decade. The Shaws reopened it as J&M’s Midtown Cafe in 2023.

Most popular dish: The simplest dish has the biggest fan base: Two Eggs – And You’re Outta Here! comes with two eggs cooked any style, hash browns and toast.

What they can never take off the menu: The Country Benedict, a warm baguette topped with two eggs, bacon, mushrooms, spinach, oven-dried tomatoes and housemade hollandaise. A staple on the Dierk’s menu, it remains a favorite among regulars.

Fun fact: The kitchen goes through about 1,500 eggs per week, or 125 dozen.

The vibe: A relaxed neighborhood diner, with a small wraparound counter for those looking for a quick meal. Inside, there’s a steady clink of forks, friendly chatter and steaming cups of Bella Rosa coffee at nearly every table. Service is casual but attentive. Joel might be cooking, taking an order or clearing tables, depending on what the moment requires.

The chef’s favorite: Chicken-fried steak. Joel judges every diner he visits by the dish. “If it’s not good, I don’t need to go back there,” he said. His version features a crisp crust over beefsteak, finished with white country sausage gravy made with turkey broth.

The deals: Bottomless mimosas on Saturdays and Sundays. All-day happy hour Mondays and Tuesdays, with $3 off alcoholic drinks.

The price: Most dishes range from $14 to $20.

The nights: On Friday evenings, Twilight Magic, a takeout-only pop-up, takes over the cafe with crispy chicken tenders, biscuits, cute-as-a-button cakelets and super-craveable Thai tea rice pudding. Emilio Saldaña makes the oversize tenders, coating them in a secret blend of herbs and spices that would make the Colonel envious, while Dia Gutierrez handles the baking. Find more details at twilight-magic-cafe.com.

Best bets

Country Benedict ($16): The benchmark against which I measure other Benedicts. Poached eggs spill their yolks over bacon, mushrooms and spinach on a split baguette, with well-balanced hollandaise and an oven-roasted tomato adding a note of acidity.

Chicken-fried steak ($19): A diner worth its salt knows how to handle this old-school favorite, a crisp, fried steak under a blanket of sausage gravy. Plenty of places serve it, but few make everything from scratch. At J&M’s, that’s more than a point of pride. It is the point.

Smoked salmon latkes Benedict ($18): Crisp on the outside and soft on the inside, the latkes are topped with house-smoked salmon rather than lox.

French toast ($12.65): Ciabatta soaked in cinnamon custard, soft in the middle and crisp around the edges.

New York-style pastrami sandwich ($16): Not quite a Reuben, but close enough. Buttery, toasted whole-grain bread holds thinly sliced pastrami, lightly pickled red cabbage and Thousand Island-style dressing. A layer of melted Jack cheese finishes the sandwich, with just enough heat to curl the pastrami’s edges. Perfection.

J&M’s Midtown Cafe is open 7 a.m. to 1:30 p.m. Thursday through Tuesday (closed Wednesday). 1422 Fourth St., Santa Rosa. 707-545-2233, jm-midtowncafe.com
